cases.title: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour
cases.stem: Mrs. Jasmine Thomas is in active labour at 39 weeks and is receiving oxytocin augmentation. Over the last 20 minutes the nurse notices repeated fetal heart rate decelerations that begin after the peak of each contraction and return to baseline after the contraction has ended. The mother is anxious and tired. Maternal vital signs are stable, contractions are strong and regular, and the fetal strip shows a concerning pattern. The nurse recognises late decelerations as potentially indicating uteroplacental insufficiency. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which description best identifies late decelerations?

options.text: Decelerations that begin after the contraction peak and recover after the contraction ends
A reassuring fetal pattern
Decelerations that mirror the contraction exactly
Abrupt drops associated with cord compression

questions.rationale: Late decelerations start after the peak of the contraction and recover after it ends. This timing is the key identifying feature and usually reflects impaired uteroplacental perfusion. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation of repeated late decelerations?

options.text: Normal pushing pattern
Reassuring fetal adaptation
Fetal oxygenation concern related to uteroplacental insufficiency
Maternal anxiety only

questions.rationale: Late decelerations are abnormal because they suggest the fetus is not tolerating contractions well, often due to decreased oxygen transfer. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Room temperature discomfort
Need for breastfeeding education
Maternal boredom
Potential fetal compromise due to reduced placental oxygen exchange

questions.rationale: The fetus is the most immediate concern here. The nurse must intervene to improve oxygen delivery and reduce stress on the fetus. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Encourage the mother to push harder
Delay action until the next shift
Reposition the mother, reduce or stop oxytocin as indicated by protocol, support oxygenation, and increase maternal-fetal assessment
Leave the oxytocin unchanged and ignore the tracing

questions.rationale: Intrauterine resuscitation measures include maternal repositioning, addressing oxytocin-driven uterine stress, supporting oxygenation, and close monitoring. This is a classic NCLEX maternity priority question. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare for further intervention if the pattern persists
Assess maternal blood pressure and contraction pattern
Consider an IV fluid bolus if indicated or ordered
Notify the provider or midwife of the non-reassuring pattern
Continue to label the pattern as normal to calm the patient

questions.rationale: The nurse must address reversible causes and escalate appropriately. Falsely labelling the pattern as normal would be unsafe and misleading. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Fetal Heart Rate Late Decelerations during Labour | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that the interventions are effective?

options.text: Decelerations worsen while oxytocin continues unchanged
The mother remains uninformed and distressed
Fetal tracing is not reassessed after repositioning
Late decelerations reduce or resolve and fetal tracing becomes more reassuring

questions.rationale: The goal of intervention is a more reassuring fetal pattern. The nurse must evaluate whether intrauterine resuscitation is working and escalate if it is not.

cases.title: Umbilical Cord Prolapse
cases.stem: Mrs. Catherine George is in labour at 38 weeks. Shortly after spontaneous rupture of membranes, the fetal heart rate suddenly drops deeply and does not recover normally. On rapid assessment, the nurse suspects umbilical cord prolapse. The patient is frightened and asks what is happening. The fetal tracing remains concerning. The nurse understands that compression of the prolapsed cord can rapidly compromise fetal oxygenation and requires immediate action. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Umbilical Cord Prolapse | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings suggest possible cord prolapse? Select all that apply.

options.text: Abrupt severe decelerations
Ongoing non-reassuring fetal tracing
Sudden fetal bradycardia after rupture of membranes
Need for rapid intrauterine resuscitation
Timing immediately after membranes rupture

questions.rationale: Cord prolapse is classically suspected when severe fetal heart rate compromise occurs immediately after rupture of membranes. The sequence of events is highly important in the diagnosis. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Umbilical Cord Prolapse | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Probable umbilical cord compression/prolapse causing acute fetal hypoxia risk
Reassuring labour progression
Normal maternal anxiety response
Postpartum complication

questions.rationale: The problem is urgent fetal compromise from cord compression. NCLEX expects immediate recognition because delay can be catastrophic. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Umbilical Cord Prolapse | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Maternal sleep deprivation
Acute interruption of fetal oxygen delivery due to cord compression
Breastfeeding readiness
Need for newborn bath preparation

questions.rationale: The fetus is at immediate risk because the compressed cord limits oxygenated blood flow. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Umbilical Cord Prolapse | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Leave the patient to find paperwork first
Delay intervention until contractions slow
Call for help, relieve pressure from the presenting part as indicated, reposition the patient urgently, and prepare for emergency birth
Encourage the patient to sit upright and push

questions.rationale: Relieving cord compression and summoning urgent obstetric help are the priorities. Time is critical, and the nurse must act immediately. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Umbilical Cord Prolapse | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Clear communication with the patient and team
Assuming the tracing will normalise without action
Continuous fetal monitoring
Preparation for urgent operative birth if indicated
Maintaining interventions that reduce cord compression

questions.rationale: Every minute matters in cord prolapse. Ongoing monitoring, communication, decompression, and preparation for emergency birth are all correct. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Umbilical Cord Prolapse | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates that nursing management is helping while definitive delivery is arranged?

options.text: Fetal heart rate improves or is better maintained while pressure is relieved and the team prepares for urgent birth
The patient is left uninformed and alone
No further monitoring is done after the first response
Fetal tracing worsens while interventions are stopped

questions.rationale: Improved or better-maintained fetal status while emergency delivery is organised shows that decompression efforts are helping.

cases.title: Shoulder Dystocia
cases.stem: Mrs. Amy Wilson is in the second stage of labour and the fetal head has just delivered. However, the head retracts tightly against the perineum and the shoulders fail to deliver with gentle downward guidance. The birth team quickly recognises possible shoulder dystocia. The mother is exhausted and frightened, and the nurse must help coordinate the emergency response while understanding that forceful traction may injure both mother and infant. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Shoulder Dystocia | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings suggest shoulder dystocia? Select all that apply.

options.text: Retraction of the fetal head against the perineum
Risk of fetal hypoxia and birth injury
Need for urgent manoeuvres
Head delivers but shoulders do not follow
Birth process suddenly stalls

questions.rationale: These findings strongly indicate shoulder dystocia. The retraction of the head, often called the turtle sign, is a classic cue. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Shoulder Dystocia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Shoulder dystocia requiring immediate coordinated obstetric manoeuvres
Normal labour delay
Postpartum haemorrhage
Placenta previa

questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia is an obstetric emergency because the impacted shoulder can prevent delivery and compromise fetal oxygenation. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Shoulder Dystocia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Need for discharge teaching
Risk for fetal hypoxia and traumatic birth injury
Sleep deprivation
Maternal thirst

questions.rationale: The urgency lies in relieving the shoulder impaction to allow delivery and prevent hypoxia or injury. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Shoulder Dystocia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Leave the room to call family
Pull forcefully on the fetal head
Call for help immediately and assist with emergency manoeuvres according to the provider’s direction
Delay action until the next contraction

questions.rationale: Shoulder dystocia requires immediate team response and use of recognised manoeuvres. Forceful traction can cause serious injury and is inappropriate. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Shoulder Dystocia | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare equipment and personnel for neonatal assessment after birth
Maintain calm communication with the team
Provide clear, focused support to the mother
Anticipate possible maternal trauma or postpartum bleeding after delivery
Assume the infant will always be fine after delivery

questions.rationale: The nurse must think beyond the moment of delivery and anticipate neonatal and maternal complications. Calm teamwork is essential. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Shoulder Dystocia | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective emergency management?

options.text: The nurse stops monitoring after the infant is born
Delivery remains stalled with no coordinated response
Maternal assessment is ignored after delivery
The infant is delivered, immediate neonatal assessment occurs, and the mother is assessed for trauma and bleeding

questions.rationale: Successful management includes safe delivery and immediate follow-up care for both mother and infant.

cases.title: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony
cases.stem: Mrs. Riya Sharma has just delivered vaginally 30 minutes ago. The nurse notices that she is bleeding more heavily than expected, soaking pads rapidly. She says she feels weak and dizzy. On palpation, the uterus feels boggy and enlarged above the expected level. Her blood pressure is 92/58 mmHg, pulse 122 beats per minute, and she appears pale. The nurse recognises likely postpartum haemorrhage caused by uterine atony. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings indicate postpartum haemorrhage with uterine atony? Select all that apply.

options.text: Heavy vaginal bleeding
Dizziness and weakness
Pallor
Boggy enlarged uterus
Tachycardia and low blood pressure

questions.rationale: These are hallmark findings of postpartum haemorrhage. A boggy uterus suggests uterine atony, one of the most common causes of PPH. Hemodynamic changes show significant blood loss. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Retained urine only
Postpartum haemorrhage likely caused by uterine atony
Normal postpartum lochia
Normal fatigue after delivery

questions.rationale: This bleeding exceeds normal lochia and is associated with a soft, enlarged uterus and unstable vital signs. NCLEX maternity care requires rapid recognition of uterine atony as an emergency. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Risk for hypovolemic shock from postpartum blood loss
Need for infant bathing teaching
Mild discomfort from contractions
Sleep deprivation

questions.rationale: Severe blood loss threatens maternal perfusion and can lead quickly to shock. That is the immediate priority. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Focus only on breastfeeding support
Send the patient to shower
Massage the fundus, call for assistance, assess bleeding, and prepare uterotonic therapy as prescribed
Delay action because bleeding is common after birth

questions.rationale: Fundal massage and urgent support are initial priorities in uterine atony. The nurse must not minimise heavy bleeding because postpartum haemorrhage can deteriorate rapidly. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Prepare IV fluids and medications as ordered
Continue to assess lochia and uterine tone
Monitor vital signs frequently
Ignore the patient’s dizziness if bleeding seems to slow briefly
Evaluate bladder distention because a full bladder can worsen atony

questions.rationale: PPH requires repeated reassessment. Bladder distention can interfere with uterine contraction. Dizziness remains clinically important and should not be dismissed. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Hemorrhage due to Uterine Atony | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates effective management?

options.text: Monitoring stops because the fundus was massaged once
The uterus becomes firm, bleeding decreases, vital signs begin to stabilise, and the patient feels less dizzy
The uterus remains boggy and bleeding continues
The patient becomes more hypotensive without escalation

questions.rationale: A firm fundus, reduced bleeding, and improved hemodynamic status show effective control of uterine atony.

cases.title: Postpartum Endometritis
cases.stem: Mrs. Linda Fernandes is two days postpartum after a prolonged labour and operative vaginal birth. She now reports chills, lower abdominal pain, and foul-smelling lochia. She says she feels hot and unwell, and she winces when the uterus is palpated. Her temperature is 38.8 C, pulse 112 beats per minute, and the uterus is tender. The nurse suspects postpartum endometritis. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Endometritis | Difficulty: Simple

questions.title: Recognise cues
questions.stem: Which findings support endometritis? Select all that apply.

options.text: Uterine tenderness
Foul-smelling lochia
Fever
Chills and malaise
Tachycardia

questions.rationale: All findings are consistent with postpartum uterine infection. Risk factors include prolonged labour and invasive or operative birth. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Endometritis | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Analyse cues
questions.stem: What is the best interpretation?

options.text: Baby blues
Normal postpartum healing
Breast engorgement only
Postpartum endometritis requiring prompt treatment

questions.rationale: The symptoms suggest uterine infection, not normal recovery. Prompt treatment is needed to prevent progression to sepsis. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Endometritis | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Prioritise hypothesis
questions.stem: Which problem is most urgent?

options.text: Minor perineal discomfort
Disturbed sleep
Infection with risk of systemic spread
Need for newborn bath education

questions.rationale: The main concern is infection and possible systemic deterioration if untreated. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Endometritis | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Take action
questions.stem: What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Delay treatment until fever is rechecked tomorrow
Ignore the odour because lochia can vary
Assess thoroughly, obtain needed cultures as ordered, and prepare for prescribed antibiotic therapy while monitoring maternal status
Encourage discharge home immediately

questions.rationale: The nurse should support timely diagnosis and treatment. Foul-smelling lochia and uterine tenderness are not normal findings to dismiss. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Endometritis | Difficulty: Difficult

questions.title: Advanced decision
questions.stem: Which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

options.text: Watch for worsening signs of sepsis
Assess lochia and uterine tenderness trends
Encourage hydration and rest as clinically appropriate
Monitor temperature and vital signs closely
Ignore the patient’s pain if antibiotics are started

questions.rationale: Close monitoring remains important even after treatment starts. Pain and sepsis risk both require ongoing reassessment. Program Area: Maternal and Newborn Nursing | Level: Level 3 - Global Nursing Professional | Section: Postpartum Endometritis | Difficulty: Moderate

questions.title: Evaluate outcomes
questions.stem: Which finding best indicates improvement?

options.text: Fever decreases, lochia becomes less offensive, uterine tenderness lessens, and the patient feels stronger
Tachycardia worsens with ongoing pain
No reassessment occurs after antibiotics begin
Fever rises and confusion develops

questions.rationale: Improvement is shown by reduction in infection signs and better overall maternal wellbeing.
